report.source_text: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the abdomen was pursued to further investigate the double duct sign, which did not reveal choledocholithiasis or pancreaticobiliary malignancy. The dilated biliary tree was suspected to be secondary to thickened descending duodenum. This thickening was abutting the hepatic flexure. Additional findings included hydroureteronephrosis on the right with a focally enhancing soft tissue mass (Fig. 3).

clinician.final_diagnosis: gastric outlet obstruction due to duodenal wall circumferential thickening with adjacent inflammatory stranding from transitional cell carcinoma metastasis
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 73-year-old male with prior stage IV transitional cell carcinoma presented with 5 weeks of nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. CT abdomen revealed circumferential duodenal wall thickening and inflammatory stranding adjacent to the hepatic flexure with signs of obstruction (double duct sign) (E001). MRI excluded pancreaticobiliary malignancy and confirmed duodenal thickening as cause of biliary dilation and obstruction (E002). Upper endoscopy showed duodenal stenosis with edema and congestion but biopsies were nondiagnostic (E003). Colonoscopy identified a hepatic flexure mass with biopsy confirming invasive transitional cell carcinoma (E004). The clinical picture, imaging, and adjacent colonic metastasis support duodenal involvement causing gastric outlet obstruction. The patient received duodenal stenting for palliation, planned chemotherapy, but deteriorated and died within one month (E005). No repeat biopsy or direct histopathological confirmation of duodenal metastasis was documented.
